lines.text: Two timbers meet end to end. The upper one drops in from above: a head on a narrow neck slides down into a socket, and the timber comes to rest on a seat.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: This is the koshikake kama-tsugi. In English, it's usually called a gooseneck splice.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress. Say 'kama-tsugi' as four short, even syllables: ka-ma-tsu-gi, with a hard g as in 'give'. Say 'koshikake' as ko-shi-ka-ke, four short even syllables.

lines.text: Two dictionaries read it kama-tsugi, and it's often shortened to just kama. On its own, kama means a sickle. But the sources tie the name to kamakubi: the way a snake raises its head and neck.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress. Say 'kama-tsugi' as four short, even syllables: ka-ma-tsu-gi, with a hard g as in 'give'. Say 'kah-mah' as two short syllables, and 'kah-mah-koo-bee' as four short even syllables.
lines.tts: Two dictionaries read it kama-tsugi, and it's often shortened to just kah-mah. On its own, kah-mah means a sickle. But the sources tie the name to kah-mah-koo-bee: the way a snake raises its head and neck.

lines.text: Gooseneck is an English name, not a translation. Nothing in the Japanese mentions geese.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: Like the dovetail splice in episode five, there's a male piece, the upper one, and a female, the lower one. The head and its socket take about the upper half of the depth. The lower half is the seat, the koshikake.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress. Say 'kama-tsugi' as four short, even syllables: ka-ma-tsu-gi, with a hard g as in 'give'. Say 'koshikake' as ko-shi-ka-ke, four short even syllables.

lines.text: A narrow neck carries a wider head at its end. A glossary's labelled drawing calls the head kama, and the neck kubi.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress. Say 'kama-tsugi' as four short, even syllables: ka-ma-tsu-gi, with a hard g as in 'give'. Say 'koo-bee' as two short syllables.

lines.text: It goes together like the dovetail. The male drops straight down and rests on the seat. Pull along the timbers, and the back of the head catches against the socket. In our model, it can't slide sideways either. Nothing stops it lifting, though.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: The proportions on screen come from one test series on hundred-and-twenty millimeter timbers. No carpentry source we found gives standard sizes.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: Compared with the dovetail, the gooseneck is longer: a neck, then a head. In one national test database, the gooseneck specimens held roughly two to three times the pull of the dovetail specimens. Their timber and sizes differed, so take that as a rough guide, not a rule.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: And a longer head isn't simply stronger. Researchers found stress gathers near the neck, and one study found the depth of the timbers mattered more than the length of the splice.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: When it fails, it fails suddenly: the head or neck shears off, or the flared edges crush. The test database notes it's usually treated as a pin: it holds against a pull, but barely resists bending.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: The Flat 35 house specification offers it, alongside the dovetail splice, for sills, eaves plates and purlins. For the beams that run around a house at second-floor level, it offers the gooseneck or another splice, but not the dovetail.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: On roof beams about a hundred and twenty deep, and on second-floor floor beams, the spec adds steel straps on both faces, bolted through. On purlins, two nails.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: On a sill, as in episode five, the anchor bolt goes in the upper piece, beside the splice.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: A short stub tenon is sometimes added under the seat. It resists twisting, but in two test series it added no pulling strength.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: And knots or short grain at the splice weaken it. The test database advises a generous safety margin, or added hardware.
